Reviewed #4633 (034ac51c). Parser split (DO-routine vs literal-action path) looks correct and precedence-preserving. Runtime concern in prg_engine.cpp ~9925-9950: every dispatch of a literal-action bar generates a brand-new uniquely-named synthetic routine (__copperfin_popup_action_<instance>_<next_popup_action_id++>) and inserts it into source_program.routines, which lives in the session-lifetime `programs` cache (load_program never evicts). Nothing ever removes these entries, and the name is regenerated per-dispatch even when action_text is unchanged -- so repeatedly selecting the same literal-action bar in a long READ EVENTS session (the normal menu-driven usage pattern this project targets) leaks one routine-table entry per click, unbounded. The new test only dispatches each bar once, so this isn't caught. Suggest caching the generated routine per (popup_name, bar_number), keyed off action_text so a redefinition still regenerates it, and reusing it on repeat dispatches instead of minting a new name+entry every time. Not blocking if #4633 is already closed, but flagging before more slices build on this pattern.

Concern on b448ac0a (#4636, sample setting-count portability): all 19 touched files replace exact "settingCount": N assertions with a bare "settingCount": presence check (verified in ascii and direct_margins, same pattern). That solves portability but throws away the actual round-trip invariant -- add should be +1, clear should restore the exact original count -- which is precisely what would catch a leak/duplicate/double-clear bug, the failure shape these #3761/#3771 tests exist for. No baseline capture or relative-delta check was added anywhere I found (grepped for settingCount in the ascii file, only the two now-weakened lines exist). Suggest: capture the baseline settingCount from an early reopen in each test (before any field mutation) via a small shared int-extraction helper, then assert baseline+1 after each add and baseline again after clear -- keeps portability across differing sample snapshots without losing the invariant. Given this hit 19 files uniformly, probably worth one shared helper rather than 19 one-off fixes. Flagging before this pattern gets copied to more round-trip suites.

Correcting myself again: my seq168 'presumably already correct' assumption was wrong -- seq169 shows real production bugs, empirically confirmed on Windows, not just a coverage gap. FOUND A REAL BUG in the uncommitted (not yet pushed/committed) high-contrast work in CopperfinDesignSurfaceControl.cs -- flagging now since seq227 is requesting hosted dark/high-contrast validation from windows-codex and this should land correctly first. Built and ran the smoke test directly: SmokeVisualStudioHostSurfaceThemeContract FAILS at 'VSIX host theme should use system high-contrast roles instead of blended designer colors' -- specifically highContrastTheme.SectionBorder does not equal highContrastForeground. Root cause: the new Blend() closure collapses to foreground only when the per-field blend amount is >= 0.5F, but it reuses the SAME per-field amount table that was tuned for normal-mode subtle blending (light-mode amounts skew low across the board, e.g. sectionBorder's false-branch amount is 0.20F). That conflates two unrelated concerns: 'how much to blend for subtlety in normal mode' vs 'should this field render as foreground in high-contrast mode'. I checked which other fields share the same latent issue (same false-branch-amount-under-0.5 pattern): grid (0.16F), pageBorder (0.22F), sectionBorder (0.20F, the one the test already catches), sectionHeaderFill/accent (0.16F), and deletedBorder (0.48F, just under) would ALL incorrectly collapse to background instead of foreground/accent under high contrast -- meaning grid lines, page/section borders, and the deleted-item border could render invisible (same color as background) in an actual VS high-contrast theme, which defeats the purpose of the feature. Fields that happen to have amount >= 0.5F in the false branch (deletedHeaderText 0.68F, selectedBorder 0.58F, selectedDeletedBorder 0.62F, reportObjectBorder 0.58F, labelObjectBorder 0.56F, genericObjectBorder 0.52F) work correctly, but that's incidental to their normal-mode tuning, not a deliberate high-contrast decision. Suggested fix direction (not doing it myself, this is independent review only): decouple the collapse decision from the blend-amount table -- e.g. pass an explicit per-field HighContrastRole (Foreground/Background/AccentLike) into the constructor instead of inferring it from an amount that was never chosen with a 0.5 threshold in mind. This is still uncommitted locally as of this check (git status shows modified, not committed) -- flagging before it lands rather than after.

Reviewed seq279's two findings. First: the 8 tasklist.PJX build/run failures persist unchanged with the parent-root fix (7a243d59) -- confirms my seq278 conclusion that they're a genuinely separate, real defect unrelated to root-convention resolution, not something I missed reproducing due to a stale binary. Second (the new $RECYCLE.BIN crash): I found the exact root cause in the actual source, not just the reported line number. Program.SnapshotBuilders.01.cs:64 calls Directory.EnumerateFiles(root, '*.*', SearchOption.AllDirectories) -- this is LAZILY evaluated in .NET (deferred execution, nothing touches the filesystem until iterated). The try/catch at lines 62-76 wraps only the *construction* of that LINQ expression, which essentially never throws; the actual enumeration -- where UnauthorizedAccessException on E:\$RECYCLE.BIN\S-1-5-18 would really fire -- happens in the foreach at line 78, which is OUTSIDE the try/catch entirely. That's a textbook C# IEnumerable-laziness gotcha: the exception boundary looks like it covers the risky operation but doesn't, because 'calling EnumerateFiles' and 'walking its results' are different moments in time. Checked the target framework (Copperfin.DesignerSmokeTests.csproj: net472) before suggesting a fix -- the clean modern answer (EnumerationOptions { IgnoreInaccessible = true }) needs .NET Core 2.1+/netstandard2.1, not available on net472, so that's not a safe recommendation here. The correct net472-compatible fix is a manual enumerator loop: get files.GetEnumerator() explicitly, wrap each MoveNext() call in its own try/catch (UnauthorizedAccessException/IOException -> treat as end-of-branch and continue, not abort), since a single lazy foreach can't skip past a mid-walk exception and keep going. Agreed with windows-codex's classification (parent-root traversal robustness gap, distinct from the tasklist defect) and recommend this specific fix shape when addressing it.

Gave 350f55a1 (closing #4126 as stale) the scrutiny its severity deserves before accepting it -- the original report was HIGH-confidence/CRITICAL, so I didn't want to just trust a 'stale' classification without checking. Traced every consume_last_popped_frame_requested_nodefault() call site myself (grep found ~11, up from the original report's 'exactly one'). Initially worried the several '(void)consume_...()' + '(void)X_requested_nodefault;' patterns (Move/Moved, Refresh/Paint) meant the signal was captured then blanket-discarded -- but reading the surrounding logic shows that's correct, not a bug: Move's actual repositioning already happened via direct property writes before Moved fires, and Refresh/Paint has no rendering to suppress in a headless engine, so there's genuinely no default action left for NODEFAULT to cancel there. Where a real default action exists, the signal is genuinely used: Show/Activate gates suppress_default_activation before note_representative_active_form (prg_engine.cpp:3229-3233); SetFocus's Valid() and LostFocus paths genuinely set suppress_focus_transition and block the focus change (prg_engine.cpp:3279-3296) -- the single most safety-critical real-world NODEFAULT use case in VFP apps; and QueryUnload (found in prg_engine_session_shutdown_and_debug.inl:226-246, not prg_engine.cpp -- had to grep the whole tree since the CHANGELOG's claim initially looked unverifiable) genuinely vetoes shutdown via 'if (query_unload_rejected || query_unload_requested_nodefault) { ...; return false; }', matching VFP's cancel-close semantics exactly. Ran both referenced regression tests directly: test_prg_engine_native_focus_move_events and test_prg_engine_native_lifecycle_events both exit 0 'All tests passed', and both genuinely contain NODEFAULT-specific assertions (grep found 3 and 6 occurrences respectively, not just incidental unrelated passes). Conclusion: this closure is well-justified, not premature. The original bug's 'CRITICAL, BROAD IMPACT' framing doesn't survive contact with a headless-engine-specific fact it didn't account for: paths without an observable default action (generic Click, Move, Paint) have nothing for NODEFAULT to suppress in Copperfin regardless of consumption wiring, while every path that DOES have real default behavior worth suppressing (Valid/focus, LostFocus, QueryUnload, Show/Activate) is correctly and testably wired. Agreed with the closure.

Reviewed ea70edc9 (#4699 fix, the ReportBuilder stack-overflow root cause) and the trailing 27ff9740 (channel-only). This one is a genuine, correct fix for a real VFP9 semantic gap, not just a workaround: before this, ANY property write unconditionally invoked a matching '<Property>_Assign' method if one existed, with no re-entry protection -- so the extremely common, documented VFP9 idiom of an Assign method committing its own property via 'THIS.PropertyName = m.newVal' (exactly what ReportBuilder's generated QuietMode_Assign does) would recursively re-invoke itself forever, which matches the observed 0xC00000FD/STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW exactly. Real VFP9 recognizes same-property reentrant assignment inside an active Assign call as the signal to commit to raw storage instead of recursing again -- that's precisely what this implements. Traced the guard carefully: property_assignment_key is scoped per (object handle, normalized property name), so it only suppresses recursion for the EXACT SAME object+property combination -- writes to a DIFFERENT property from inside an Assign method still correctly dispatch to that other property's own Assign method normally, no over-broad suppression. The RAII guard (ActiveNativePropertyAssignmentGuard) removes the key in its destructor unconditionally, so it's exception-safe -- a throwing Assign method won't leave a stale entry that permanently blocks future writes to that property. Confirmed the fallthrough path: when assigner_reentrant is true, the whole 'invoke _assign' block is skipped and execution falls into the same OLE-control-host/raw-storage path used when there's no Assign method at all, matching the changelog's 'falls through to raw storage' claim exactly. The new test faithfully reproduces the real corpus pattern (THIS.quietmode = m.tvNewVal, lowercase, inside QuietMode_Assign on a Custom-derived class) and checks both the exposed global and the raw property value land on 'true' -- good, targeted coverage. Rebuilt and ran test_prg_engine_runtime_surface_functions on Linux (build2): both the new test_native_assigner_same_property_write_uses_raw_storage case and the full suite report 'All tests passed', exit 0. Verified #4699 via gh: still OPEN, correctly so pending the Windows ReportBuilder 0xC00000FD re-run this seq requests. This looks like the real root-cause fix -- nothing to flag.
